```{r setup, include = FALSE}
  collapse = TRUE,

library(SMSD)
term <- function(x, name) x$value[x$term == name]
fixed <- function(x, digits) formatC(x, digits = digits, format = "f")
```

## The Research Question

The coefficient of variation, κ = σ / μ, expresses the standard deviation
of a quantity relative to its mean, so it summarizes dispersion on a unit
free scale. It is used wherever relative, rather than absolute,
variability is the quantity of interest: the relative variability of
assay measurements in the laboratory, of claim sizes in insurance, of
response times in an experiment, or of household expenditures in survey
research.

How many observations should be collected to estimate κ well? When each
observation carries a cost (a record to audit, a participant to run, a
sample to assay), collecting more data buys a more accurate estimate and
spends more of the study budget. Minimum risk point estimation (MRPE)
makes that trade explicit. Chattopadhyay and Kelley (2016) develop a
purely sequential procedure that estimates κ while minimizing a risk that
combines estimation error and sampling cost. Because the asymptotic
variance of the sample coefficient of variation depends on the unknown
population (through its third and fourth moments), the sample size cannot
be fixed in advance; the data collected so far say whether to stop.

## The Method

Write *k*<sub>*n*</sub> for the sample coefficient of variation after
*n* observations, the sample standard deviation divided by the sample
mean. The risk combines the expected squared estimation error, priced by
a constant *A*, with the cost *c* of each observation (Equation 11 of
Chattopadhyay and Kelley, 2016):

<p style="text-align: center;"><i>R</i><sub><i>n</i></sub>(&kappa;) = <i>A</i> E[(<i>k</i><sub><i>n</i></sub> &minus; &kappa;)<sup>2</sup>] + <i>c</i> <i>n</i></p>

For samples that are not too small the mean squared error is
approximately ξ<sup>2</sup> / *n*, where ξ<sup>2</sup> is the asymptotic
variance of √*n* (*k*<sub>*n*</sub> − κ), so the risk is approximately
*A* ξ<sup>2</sup> / *n* + *c* *n* (their Equation 14). That is smallest at
the optimal fixed sample size (their Equation 15)

<p style="text-align: center;"><i>n</i><sub><i>c</i></sub> = (<i>A</i> / <i>c</i>)<sup>1/2</sup> &xi;</p>

where it equals 2 *c* *n*<sub>*c*</sub> (their Equation 16). Because
ξ<sup>2</sup> is unknown, the purely sequential rule estimates it from the
data after each observation; write *V*<sub>*n*</sub><sup>2</sup> for the
estimate from the first *n*. To keep a low early estimate from stopping
the procedure too soon, a small correction term is added, and sampling
stops at the first *n* at or beyond the pilot sample size with (their
Equation 23)

<p style="text-align: center;"><i>n</i><sup>2</sup> &ge; (<i>A</i> / <i>c</i>) (<i>V</i><sub><i>n</i></sub><sup>2</sup> + <i>n</i><sup>&minus;2&gamma;</sup>)</p>

where γ is a constant strictly between 0 and 1/2 (the article suggests
0.49, the default of the argument `gamma`). The pilot sample size is the
larger of a minimum *m*<sub>0</sub> and (*A* / *c*)<sup>1/(2 + 2γ)</sup>,
rounded up (their Equation 24, a form the article gives as following
Mukhopadhyay and de Silva, 2009).

## The Sequential Workflow

`seq_mr_cv_pilot()` returns the pilot sample size, which depends only on
the two cost constants, and `seq_mr_cv()` evaluates the stopping rule on
the data collected so far and records the decision as an attribute.
Neither collects data or keeps state: the analyst calls `seq_mr_cv()`
again after each new observation. There is no confidence level, because
the procedure targets a risk and not a confidence interval.

Suppose an actuary is estimating the relative variability of individual
claim amounts (in thousands of dollars), which are positive and heavily
right skewed. Auditing one claim costs one unit, and a unit of squared
estimation error is priced at *A* = 900.

```{r pilot}
A <- 900      # price of one unit of squared estimation error
cost <- 1     # cost of auditing one claim record
pilot_n <- seq_mr_cv_pilot(A = A, c = cost)
pilot_n
```

To have data to work with, 100 claims are simulated here from a right
skewed gamma distribution whose coefficient of variation is
`r fixed(1 / sqrt(0.6), 2)`; they stand for the claims in the order they
would be audited. The actuary audits the pilot sample and evaluates the
rule.

```{r first-check}
set.seed(113)
claims <- rgamma(100, shape = 0.6, scale = 2)
check <- seq_mr_cv(claims[1:pilot_n], A = A, c = cost)
check
```

The criterion sample size implied by the pilot data exceeds the pilot
sample size, so the rule is not met and auditing continues, one claim at
a time, with a new check after each. In a study that is a call to
`seq_mr_cv()` after each claim. With the claims already in hand,
`seq_path()` makes the same sequence of checks in one call, and its plot
shows the criterion moving as the claims arrive.

```{r path, fig.alt = "Current sample size, a rising straight line, and criterion sample size, a fluctuating line, against the number of claims audited; the two first meet at the stopping point."}
path <- seq_path(seq_mr_cv, claims, A = A, c = cost)
attr(path, "stop_n")
plot(path, which = "criterion")
attr(path, "final_check")
```

The rule was first met at `r attr(path, "stop_n")` claims, and that is
where the audit ends: the estimate a sequential design reports is the one
at the stopping point, not one from a later, more favorable sample size.
The reported `cv` is the minimum risk point estimate of κ, and `risk` is
the estimated risk there. MRPE returns a point estimate and no confidence
interval, and the estimate carries the sampling error of a statistic
computed at a modest sample size. `seq_report()` words the result for a
methods section:

```{r report}
seq_report(path)
```

Two situations are reported as "not met" whatever the sample size. If the
variance estimate is zero, negative, or not finite (every observation so
far is the same, or the sample gives a negative estimate), no variance has
been estimated: the rule is reported as not met, the result carries
`attr(check, "variance_unusable")` equal to `TRUE`, and a note is printed
(see "An Unusable Variance Estimate" in `help("SMSD-package")`). Read
literally, the article's rule would stop
at once on such an estimate; the package departs from it on purpose. A
positive estimate, however small, is used as the articles prescribe
(bounded below by *n*<sup>−3</sup>), so a small coefficient of variation,
or a change in the units of the data, does not by itself make the estimate
unusable. If the sample mean is zero or negative (or differs from zero
only by rounding error, as for centered or standardized scores), the
coefficient of variation cannot be estimated, and the result says so.

The first of these departures costs little when a negative estimate is
rare, as it is for normal data: with a coefficient of variation of 0.10,
*A* = 400, and *c* = 1 (a pilot sample size of 8), the mean final sample
size in 2,000 simulated runs was 8.05, where the rule as printed gave
8.00. It can cost a great deal for a quantity that takes only two or
three distinct values and has a small coefficient of variation, because
the estimate is then negative at many stages in a row. With observations
equal to 9 or 11 with equal probability and the same constants, the rule
as printed stopped at 8 in every run; `seq_mr_cv()` stopped at 8 in about
half of the runs and kept sampling in the rest, to a mean final sample
size of 25, a 99th percentile of 244, and a largest value of 693. For a
quantity of that kind, decide on a largest sample size before sampling
begins. (These figures are from the simulations reported in
`?seq_mr_cv`.)

## Two Variance Estimators

The argument `variance` of `seq_mr_cv()` selects the estimator
*V*<sub>*n*</sub><sup>2</sup>.

The default, `variance = "corrected"`, is the estimator of Kelley, Darku,
and Chattopadhyay (2018, Equations 31 and 32), the sample version of the
asymptotic variance of the coefficient of variation for a general
population (their Equation 30),

<p style="text-align: center;">&xi;<sup>2</sup> = &mu;<sub>4</sub> / (4 &mu;<sup>2</sup> &sigma;<sup>2</sup>) &minus; &sigma;<sup>2</sup> / (4 &mu;<sup>2</sup>) &minus; &mu;<sub>3</sub> / &mu;<sup>3</sup> + &sigma;<sup>4</sup> / &mu;<sup>4</sup></p>

where μ<sub>3</sub> and μ<sub>4</sub> are the third and fourth central
moments. It is the estimator that `seq_aipe_cv()` uses.

The alternative, `variance = "published"`, is Equation 22 of Chattopadhyay
and Kelley (2016), the sample version of their Equation 9,

<p style="text-align: center;">&mu;<sub>4</sub> / (4 &mu;<sup>4</sup>) + &sigma;<sup>4</sup> / (4 &mu;<sup>4</sup>) &minus; &mu;<sub>3</sub> / &mu;<sup>3</sup> + &sigma;<sup>2</sup> / (2 &mu;<sup>2</sup>)</p>

The first expression minus the second is κ<sup>2</sup> (1 −
κ<sup>2</sup>) / 4 times the excess kurtosis, μ<sub>4</sub> /
σ<sup>4</sup> − 3. The two are therefore the same for a normal
population, and for any population with no excess kurtosis, and they
differ otherwise. For a population with heavier tails than the normal and
κ below 1 the published expression is the smaller of the two, so the
procedure stops before the sample size that minimizes the risk. For a
gamma population with κ = 0.8:

```{r two-variances}
shape <- 1 / 0.8^2                    # gamma, unit scale: kappa = 0.8
mu <- shape
sigma2 <- shape
mu3 <- 2 * shape                      # third central moment
mu4 <- 3 * shape * (shape + 2)        # fourth central moment
xi2 <- c(
  corrected = mu4 / (4 * mu^2 * sigma2) - sigma2 / (4 * mu^2) -
    mu3 / mu^3 + sigma2^2 / mu^4,
  published = mu4 / (4 * mu^4) + sigma2^2 / (4 * mu^4) -
    mu3 / mu^3 + sigma2 / (2 * mu^2)
)
xi2
kappa2 <- sigma2 / mu^2               # the difference, and the identity
c(difference = xi2[["corrected"]] - xi2[["published"]],
  identity = kappa2 * (1 - kappa2) / 4 * (mu4 / sigma2^2 - 3))
sqrt(5000000 / 10 * xi2)              # the sample size each one aims at
```

Simulation shows which expression describes the estimator. In 200,000
samples of 400 observations from that population, *n* times the mean
squared error of *k*<sub>*n*</sub> was 0.516 (standard error 0.002),
beside the `r fixed(xi2[["corrected"]], 3)` and
`r fixed(xi2[["published"]], 3)` just computed. In the full procedure
with *A* = 5,000,000 and *c* = 10, for which the risk is smallest at
`r fixed(sqrt(5000000 / 10 * xi2[["corrected"]]), 0)` observations, the
mean final sample size in 5,000 replications was 479 with the corrected
estimator and about 374 with the published one. (Both simulations are
reported in the Details of `?seq_mr_cv`.) Table 1 of the article (p. 642)
reports 374.0 for this population, beside an optimal sample size of 390,
which is the value the published expression gives.

Use the default. The published estimator is offered so that the article's
worked example and tables, and the results of `mr_cv()` in `DMAR` and
`mr.cv()` in `MBESS` (which use the published form), can be reproduced.
The derivation of both expressions by the delta method, with the algebra
written out and a simulation a reader can run, is in a note installed
with the package:

```{r note-file}
file.exists(system.file("cv_variance_note.md", package = "SMSD"))
```

## Reproducing the Published Example

Chattopadhyay and Kelley (2016, pp. 637 to 638) estimate the coefficient
of variation of the number of age appropriate books in the homes of third
graders. A home visit costs 75 dollars, and the team would pay 1,000
dollars to estimate κ to within 0.05, so *A* = 1,000 / 0.05<sup>2</sup> =
400,000. The pilot sample size is 18.

```{r published-pilot}
seq_mr_cv_pilot(A = 400000, c = 75)
```

With the article's own variance, the 18 pilot observations give the risk
and estimate printed in the article (5964.345 and 0.7391157), and the rule
is not met.

```{r published-18}
books <- c(36, 53, 19, 11, 10, 24, 14, 65, 18, 48, 25, 35, 13, 18, 3, 41,
           5, 3, 44, 26, 13, 39, 2, 3, 26, 22, 8, 15, 12, 22, 5, 21, 23,
           40, 18)
seq_mr_cv(books[1:18], A = 400000, c = 75, variance = "published")
```

The article adds observations one at a time, and the rule is met for the
first time at the 35th, with risk 4891.284.

```{r published-35}
published <- seq_path(seq_mr_cv, books, A = 400000, c = 75,
                      variance = "published")
attr(published, "stop_n")
attr(published, "final_check")
```

With the default variance the same 35 observations never meet the rule
(`stop_n` is `NA`); the criterion at the 35th asks for one more.

```{r default-35}
corrected <- seq_path(seq_mr_cv, books, A = 400000, c = 75)
attr(corrected, "stop_n")
attr(corrected, "final_check")
```

## What to Expect Before the Study

`seq_mr_cv_sensitivity()` runs the whole procedure many times on simulated
data with a known coefficient of variation and compares the result with
the best fixed sample size. For the actuary's problem, with gamma claims
whose coefficient of variation is 1.3:

```{r sensitivity}
sens <- seq_mr_cv_sensitivity(true_value = 1.3, A = A, c = cost,
                              distribution = "gamma", G = 500, seed = 2016)
sens
```

`optimal_n` is the fixed sample size that minimizes the large sample risk
for this population, and `minimum_risk` is the risk there. `ratio_n`
compares the mean final sample size with the optimum, and
`risk_efficiency` compares the mean realized loss with the minimum risk;
it should be read against its Monte Carlo standard error,
`se_risk_efficiency`.

The result is a caution about small studies of heavily skewed quantities.
With *A* = 900 the procedure takes about
`r fixed(term(sens, "mean_n"), 0)` claims on average, where the best fixed
sample size is `r fixed(term(sens, "optimal_n"), 0)`. The variance
estimate rests on the third and fourth sample moments, which are very
variable in small samples from a population this skewed, and sampling
ends the first time the criterion is met, so a low estimate ends it early.
The guarantees of the procedure are asymptotic: the ratio approaches 1 as
*A* / *c* grows, but slowly here. In the runs reported in the Details of
`?seq_mr_cv`, for the same population and cost, the ratio was about 0.58,
0.74, 0.85, and 0.93 with *A* equal to 900, 9,000, 90,000, and 900,000.
The benchmark is itself a large sample approximation, which is why the
risk efficiency can fall below 1 at sample sizes this small; that does not
mean the procedure did better than the best fixed design. For a milder
population the agreement is closer: in the same Details, with
*A* = 5,000,000 and *c* = 10 (5,000 replications), the ratio was about
0.99 for gamma data with κ = 0.4, and the ratio of the realized risk to
the minimum risk was within about 0.03 of 1.

Running the same call with `variance = "published"`,
`distribution = "lognormal"`, or a batch size (`batch`, the number of
observations added between checks) shows how each choice changes the
picture.

## Relationship to Accuracy in Parameter Estimation

`SMSD` supports the coefficient of variation in two ways. Use
`seq_mr_cv()` when the design goal is to minimize a loss that balances
accuracy against the cost of sampling. Use `seq_aipe_cv()` when the goal
is a confidence interval of a target width, that is, accuracy in parameter
estimation through a narrow interval (Kelley, Darku, & Chattopadhyay,
2018; Maxwell, Kelley, & Rausch, 2008). With the default variance the two
procedures share one distribution free estimator of the asymptotic
variance and answer different design questions.
